title: Slides: More Groups
text:
Definition of a Group
A group \((G,\cdot)\) is a set \(G\) together with a law of composition
\((a,b)\mapsto a\cdot b\) satisfying:

Associativity:
\((a\cdot b)\cdot c=a\cdot(b\cdot c)\) for \(a,b,c\in G\).
Identity:
There exists \(e\in G\) such that \(e\cdot a=a\cdot e=a\) for every \(a\in G\).
Inverses:
For each \(a\in G\), there exists \(a^{-1}\in G\) such that \(a\cdot a^{-1}=a^{-1}\cdot a=e\).

title: Slides: More Groups
text:
Definition of a Subgroup
Let \(G\) be a group.
A subgroup \(H\) of \(G\) is a subset \(H\) of \(G\) such that when the group operation of \(G\) is restricted to \(H\), \(H\) is a group in its own right.
We write \(H \leq G\).
A subgroup uses the same operation as the original group.

title: Slides: More Groups
text:
Proposition 3.3.7 Subgroup Criterion
A subset \(H\) of \(G\) is a subgroup if and only if it satisfies the following conditions.

Identity The identity \(e\) of \(G\) is in \(H\).
Closure If \(h_1,h_2\in H\), then
\[
h_1h_2\in H.
\]
Inverse If \(h\in H\), then
\[
h^{-1}\in H.
\]

title: Slides: More Groups
text:
Proposition 3.3.8 Another Subgroup Test
Let \(H\) be a subset of a group \(G\).
Then \(H\) is a subgroup of \(G\) if and only if
\[
H\neq\emptyset
\]
and whenever \(g,h\in H\),
\[
gh^{-1}\in H.
\]

title: Slides: More Groups
text:
Proof of Second Subgroup Test
One condition gives us everything:

Identity: \(gg^{-1}=e\in H\)
Inverse: \(eg^{-1}=g^{-1}\in H\)
Closure: \(h_1(h_2^{-1})^{-1}=h_1h_2\in H\)

title: Slides: More Groups
section: Example of using the Subgroup Test
text:
Example of using the Subgroup Test
Let \(H=2\mathbb Z.\)
Since \(0\in H\), we know \(H\neq\emptyset\).
If \(a,b\in H\), then \(a=2m,\qquad b=2n\) for some \(m,n\in\mathbb Z\).
Therefore \(a-b=2m-2n=2(m-n)\in2\mathbb Z\).
Hence \(2\mathbb Z\leq\mathbb Z\).

Definition of a Group
A group \((G,\cdot)\) is a set \(G\) together with a law of composition
\((a,b)\mapsto a\cdot b\) satisfying:

Associativity:
\((a\cdot b)\cdot c=a\cdot(b\cdot c)\) for \(a,b,c\in G\).

There exists \(e\in G\) such that \(e\cdot a=a\cdot e=a\) for every \(a\in G\).
Inverses:

text:
Definition of a Subgroup
Let \(G\) be a group.
A subgroup \(H\) of \(G\) is a subset \(H\) of \(G\) such that when the group operation of \(G\) is restricted to \(H\), \(H\) is a group in its own right.
We write \(H \leq G\).

title: Slides: Multiplicative Group of Complex Numbers
text:
Complex Numbers and Operations
The complex numbers are defined as
\[
\mathbb{C}=\{a+bi:a,b\in\mathbb{R}\},
\]
where \(i^2=-1\). If \(z=a+bi\), then \(a\) is the real part of \(z\) and \(b\) is the imaginary part of \(z\).
If \(z=a+bi\) and \(w=c+di\), then
\[
z+w=(a+c)+(b+d)i.
\]
Multiplication is given by
\[
zw=(a+bi)(c+di)=(ac-bd)+(ad+bc)i.
\]
crumbs: Slides: Multiplicative Group of Complex Numbers

title: Slides: Multiplicative Group of Complex Numbers
text:
Multiplicative Inverses and Conjugates
Every nonzero complex number \(z=a+bi\) has a multiplicative inverse:
\[
z^{-1}=\frac{a-bi}{a^2+b^2}.
\]
The complex conjugate of \(z=a+bi\) is
\[
\overline{z}=a-bi.
\]
The absolute value or modulus of \(z=a+bi\) is \(|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\).
crumbs: Slides: Multiplicative Group of Complex Numbers

title: Slides: Multiplicative Group of Complex Numbers
text:
Examples
For example, if \(z=2+3i\), then
\[
z^{-1}=\frac{2}{13}-\frac{3}{13}i,
\qquad |z|=\sqrt{13},
\qquad \overline{z}=2-3i.
\]
crumbs: Slides: Multiplicative Group of Complex Numbers

title: Slides: Multiplicative Group of Complex Numbers
text:
Polar representation of Complex Numbers
Nonzero complex numbers can also be represented using polar coordinates.
\(z=a+bi=r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)\) where \(a=r\cos\theta\) and \(b=r\sin\theta\), and \(r=|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\).
Book abbreviates \(r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)\) as \(r\operatorname{cis}\theta\).
We require \(0\leq\theta<2\pi\).

Angle Addition Formulas
For \(\theta, \phi \in \mathbb{R}\),
\[
\sin(\theta+\phi)
=\sin\theta\cos\phi+\cos\theta\sin\phi
\]

\[
\cos(\theta+\phi)

\]

Let \(z=r\operatorname{cis}\theta\) and \(w=s\operatorname{cis}\phi\) be two nonzero complex numbers. Then
\[
zw=rs\operatorname{cis}(\theta+\phi).
\]

title: Slides: Multiplicative Group of Complex Numbers
text:
Example
If
\[

\qquad\text{and}\qquad
w=2\operatorname{cis}\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right),
\]

zw

\]

title: Slides: Multiplicative Group of Complex Numbers
text:
DeMoivre’s Theorem (4.2.7)
Let \(z=r\operatorname{cis}\theta\) be a nonzero complex number. Then
\[
[r\operatorname{cis}\theta]^n
=r^n\operatorname{cis}(n\theta)
\]
for \(n=1,2,\ldots\).
crumbs: Slides: Multiplicative Group of Complex Numbers

title: Slides: Multiplicative Group of Complex Numbers
text:
Example
If \(z=1+i\), then
\[
z=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cis}\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right).
\]
Thus,
\[
z^{10}
=(\sqrt{2})^{10}\operatorname{cis}\left(\frac{5\pi}{2}\right)
=32\operatorname{cis}\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)
=32i.
\]

title: Slides: Multiplicative Group of Complex Numbers
text:
\(n^{\text{th}}\) Roots of Unity
The complex numbers satisfying the equation
\[
z^n=1
\]
are called the \(n\)th roots of unity.
They lie on the unit circle and are equally spaced around the circle.
A generator for the group of the \(n\)th roots of unity is called a primitive \(n\)th root of unity.
crumbs: Slides: Multiplicative Group of Complex Numbers

title: Slides: Multiplicative Group of Complex Numbers
text:
Theorem 4.2.10
If \(z^n=1\), then the \(n\)th roots of unity are
\[
z=\operatorname{cis}\left(\frac{2k\pi}{n}\right),
\]
where \(k=0,1,\ldots,n-1\).
Furthermore, the \(n\)th roots of unity form a cyclic subgroup of \(\mathbb{T}\) of order \(n\).
crumbs: Slides: Multiplicative Group of Complex Numbers

title: Slides: Multiplicative Group of Complex Numbers
text:
Proof
By DeMoivre’s Theorem,
\[
z^n
=\operatorname{cis}\left(n\frac{2k\pi}{n}\right)
=\operatorname{cis}(2k\pi)
=1.
\]
crumbs: Slides: Multiplicative Group of Complex Numbers

title: Slides: Multiplicative Group of Complex Numbers
text:
Example 9th roots of unity
The \(9\)th roots of unity satisfy
\[
z^9=1.
\]
By Theorem 4.2.10,
\[
z_k=\operatorname{cis}\left(\frac{2k\pi}{9}\right),
\qquad k=0,1,\ldots,8.
\]
Thus the nine roots are
\[
1,\;
\operatorname{cis}\left(\frac{2\pi}{9}\right),\;
\operatorname{cis}\left(\frac{4\pi}{9}\right),\;
\operatorname{cis}\left(\frac{6\pi}{9}\right),\;
\ldots,\;
\operatorname{cis}\left(\frac{16\pi}{9}\right).
\]
They form a cyclic subgroup of \(\mathbb{T}\) of order \(9\).
For example,
\[
\omega=\operatorname{cis}\left(\frac{2\pi}{9}\right)
\]
is a primitive \(9\)th root of unity, and
\[
\langle\omega\rangle
=\{1,\omega,\omega^2,\ldots,\omega^8\}.
\]
crumbs: Slides: Multiplicative Group of Complex Numbers

title: Slides: Permutation Groups
text:
Class Session Goals

Define the symmetric group \(S_n\).
Represent permutations using cycle notation.
Compute products of permutations.
Write permutations as products of disjoint cycles and transpositions.

title: Slides: Permutation Groups
text:
What is the Symmetric Group?
A permutation of a set \(X\) is a one-to-one and onto function
\[
\sigma:X\longrightarrow X.
\]
The permutations of a set \(X\) form a group \(S_X\).
If \(X\) is finite, we can assume
\[
X=\{1,2,\ldots,n\}.
\]
In this case, we write \(S_n\) instead of \(S_X\).
The group \(S_n\) is called the symmetric group on \(n\) letters.

title: Slides: Permutation Groups
text:
Permutation Drawings
A permutation describes a rearrangement of a set.
We can represent a permutation by drawing where each element is sent.

Follow the lines in the drawing:
\[
1\mapsto2,\qquad
2\mapsto3,\qquad
3\mapsto1,\qquad
4\mapsto5,\qquad
5\mapsto4.
\]
Every element is sent to exactly one element, and every element is the image of exactly one element.

title: Slides: Permutation Groups
text:
From Drawings to Permutation Notation
We can record the same permutation without the drawing.
The top row lists the elements.
The bottom row records where each element is sent.
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
1&2&3&4&5\\
2&3&1&5&4
\end{pmatrix}
\]
The drawing and the two-line notation represent the same permutation.

title: Slides: Permutation Groups
text:
Activity: Build \(S_4\)
Today we are going to construct every element of \(S_4\).
There are $|S_4|=4!=24 permutations to construct.
For each card:

Draw the permutation by connecting the top row to the bottom row.
On the top half of the blank side, write the permutation in two-line notation.
Leave the bottom half blank — we will add different notation later.

title: Slides: Permutation Groups
section: We Have a Set — Now We Need an Operation
text:
We Have a Set — Now We Need an Operation
We have constructed the \(24\) elements of \(S_4\). How should we multiply two permutations?
Place one permutation drawing on top of another and follow the paths from top to bottom.
If \(\sigma\) is on the bottom and \(\tau\) is on the top, we write \(\sigma\tau\).
Apply the function \(\tau\) first, then \(\sigma\).
\[\sigma\tau(x)=\sigma(\tau(x))\]

title: Slides: Permutation Groups
text:
Activity: Explore Multiplication in \(S_4\)
Choose several pairs of tiles and calculate their products.
For each pair, stack the two permutation drawings. Follow \(1,2,3,4\) through both drawings. Find the tile representing the product.
Ponderings: Does your product always correspond to another tile in \(S_4\)? Can you find an indentity tile \(e\)? Can you find inverses?

title: Slides: Permutation Groups
text:
Activity: What About Associativity?
Choose three permutation tiles and call them \(\sigma,\qquad\tau,\qquad\rho\).
Calculate \((\sigma\tau)\rho\). Find the corresponding tile in \(S_4\) for \((\sigma\tau)\).
Calculate \(\sigma(\tau\rho)\). Find the corresponding tile in \(S_4\) for \((\tau\rho)\).
Compare your results are the two resulting mappings the same or different?

text:
Theorem 5.1.1
The symmetric group on \(n\) letters, \(S_n\), is a group with \(n!\) elements, where the binary operation is the composition of maps.

title: Slides: Permutation Groups
text:
Proof
Identity: Consider the permutation \(\pi(i)=i\).
Inverse: If \(\pi(i)=j\), define \(\tau(j)=i\).
Associativity: Composition of maps is associative.

title: Slides: Permutation Groups
text:
Cycle Notation
Permutation drawings show us where every element goes. Instead of recording every mapping, we can follow an element until we return to where we started.

For example, \(1\mapsto2\mapsto3\mapsto1\) is written \((1\,2\,3)\).
The other set of elements satisfies \(4\mapsto5\mapsto4\). We write \((4\,5)\).
Together, the permutation is \((1\,2\,3)(4\,5)\). This is called cycle notation.

title: Slides: Permutation Groups
text:
Reading Cycle Notation
In the cycle \((1\,3\,4\,2)\) we read from left to right:
\[
1\mapsto3,\qquad
3\mapsto4,\qquad
4\mapsto2,\qquad
2\mapsto1.
\]
Elements that do not appear in a cycle are fixed.
For example, in \(S_6\) \((1\,3\,4\,2)\)
also means \(5\mapsto5 \qquad\text{and}\qquad6\mapsto6\).

title: Slides: Permutation Groups
text:
Cycle Notation Multiplication
Let \(\sigma=(1\,3\,5)(2\,4),\qquad\tau=(1\,2\,6)(3\,4)\).
Compute \(\sigma\tau\) right to left:
\[
1\xrightarrow{\tau}2\xrightarrow{\sigma}4
\quad
4\xrightarrow{\tau}3\xrightarrow{\sigma}5
\quad
5\xrightarrow{\tau}5\xrightarrow{\sigma}1
\]
so we get \((1\,4\,5)\). Starting with \(2\):
\[
2\xrightarrow{\tau}6\xrightarrow{\sigma}6
\quad
6\xrightarrow{\tau}1\xrightarrow{\sigma}3
\quad
3\xrightarrow{\tau}4\xrightarrow{\sigma}2
\]
so we get \((2\,6\,3)\).
Therefore, \(\sigma\tau=(1\,4\,5)(2\,6\,3)\).

title: Slides: Permutation Groups
text:
Proposition 5.1.8
Let \(\sigma\) and \(\tau\) be two disjoint cycles in \(S_X\). Then \(\sigma\tau=\tau\sigma\).
If \(x\) occurs in \(\sigma\), then \(\tau\) fixes \(x\) and every element to which \(\sigma\) sends \(x\).

title: Slides: Permutation Groups
text:
Theorem 5.1.9
Every permutation in \(S_n\) can be written as the product of disjoint cycles.

title: Slides: Permutation Groups
text:
Proof
Start with \(1\) and repeatedly apply \(\sigma\):
\[
1,\sigma(1),\sigma^2(1),\ldots
\]
Since the set is finite, we eventually return to \(1\), producing a cycle.
Next, choose an element not appearing in that cycle and repeat the process.
Continuing in this manner produces disjoint cycles \(\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\ldots,\sigma_r\)
such that\(\sigma=\sigma_1\sigma_2\cdots\sigma_r\).

title: Slides: Permutation Groups
text:
Transpositions
A cycle of length \(2\) is called a transposition.
For example,\((2\,5)\) is a transposition. Any cycle can be written as a product of transpositions:
\[
(a_1\,a_2\,\ldots\,a_n)
=
(a_1\,a_n)(a_1\,a_{n-1})\cdots(a_1\,a_3)(a_1\,a_2).
\]
A permutation is even if it can be expressed as an even number of transpositions.
A permutation is odd if it can be expressed as an odd number of transpositions.

title: Slides: Permutation Groups
section: Activity: Even and Odd Permutations in \(S_4\)
text:
Activity: Even and Odd Permutations in \(S_4\)
Return to the 24 permutation tiles that make up \(S_4\).
Then sort all \(24\) tiles into two groups: odd permutation and even permutations.
Ponderings: How many permutations are even? How many permutations are odd? What types of cycles appear in each group?

title: Slides: Permutation Groups
text:
Lemma 5.1.14
If the identity is written as the product of \(r\) transpositions,
\[
\operatorname{id}=\tau_1\tau_2\cdots\tau_r,
\]
then \(r\) is an even number.

title: Slides: Permutation Groups
text:
Proof of Lemma 5.1.14
We use induction on \(r\) the number of transpositions. A transposition cannot be the identity, so \(r>1\). If \(r=2\), we are done.
For \(r>2\), consider the last two transpositions. Up to relabeling, we have
\[
\begin{aligned}
(a\,b)(a\,b)&=\operatorname{id},\\
(b\,c)(a\,b)&=(a\,c)(b\,c),\\
(c\,d)(a\,b)&=(a\,b)(c\,d),\\
(a\,c)(a\,b)&=(a\,b)(b\,c).
\end{aligned}
\]
Use these identities to move the last occurrence of \(a\) to the left.
Eventually either two identical adjacent transpositions cancel, leaving \(r-2\) transpositions, or \(a\) occurs only in the first transposition.
The second case is impossible since the product is the identity and must fix \(a\).
Thus the identity is a product of \(r-2\) transpositions. By induction, \(r-2\) is even, so \(r\) is even.

title: Slides: Permutation Groups
text:
Theorem 5.1.15
If a permutation \(\sigma\) can be expressed as the product of an even number of transpositions, then any other product of transpositions equaling \(\sigma\) must also contain an even number of transpositions.
Similarly, if \(\sigma\) can be expressed as the product of an odd number of transpositions, then any other product of transpositions equaling \(\sigma\) must also contain an odd number of transpositions.

title: Slides: Permutation Groups
text:
Alternating Group
The set of all even permutations in \(S_n\) is denoted by \(A_n\).
The group \(A_n\) is called the alternating group on \(n\) letters.
\[
A_n=\{\sigma\in S_n:\sigma\text{ is even}\}.
\]

title: Slides: Permutation Groups
text:
Theorem 5.1.16
The set \(A_n\) is a subgroup of \(S_n\).
Why?

The product of two even permutations is even.
The identity is even.
The inverse of an even permutation is even.

title: Slides: Permutation Groups
text:
Proposition 5.1.17
The number of even permutations in \(S_n\), \(n\geq2\), is equal to the number of odd permutations. So $ |A_n|=.$
Let \(A_n\) be the set of even permutations and \(B_n\) the set of odd permutations.
Fix a transposition \(\sigma\in S_n\) and define \(\lambda_\sigma:A_n\longrightarrow B_n\)
by \(\lambda_\sigma(\tau)=\sigma\tau\). Multiplication by a transposition changes the parity of a permutation. The map \(\lambda_\sigma\) is a bijection, so \(A_n\) and \(B_n\) contain the same number of elements.

title: Slides: Cyclic Groups
text:
Class Session Goals

Understand the structure of groups generated by a single element
Determine when an element generates a group

title: Slides: Cyclic Groups
text:
Generator, Notation, and Order
Let \(G\) be a group and let \(a \in G\). The subgroup generated by \(a\) is \(\langle a \rangle = \{a^n : n \in \mathbb{Z}\}\).
A group \(G\) is cyclic if there exists an element \(a \in G\) such that \(G = \langle a \rangle\).
In this case, \(a\) is called a generator of \(G\).
The order of \(a\) is the smallest positive integer \(n\) such that \(a^n=e\), if such an integer exists.

title: Slides: Cyclic Groups
section: Examples of Groups Generated by one element
text:
Examples of Groups Generated by one element
The group of integers under addition is cyclic:
\[
\mathbb{Z}=\langle 1\rangle=\langle -1\rangle.
\]
The group \(\mathbb{Z}_n\) under addition is cyclic:
\[
\mathbb{Z}_n=\langle 1\rangle.
\]
In \(U(18)\), \(\langle 5\rangle\) and \(\langle 11\rangle\) are generators, but \(\langle 7\rangle\) is not.

title: Slides: Cyclic Groups
text:
Theorem 4.1.3
Theorem. Let \(G\) be a group and \(a \in G\). Then \(\langle a \rangle = \{a^k : k \in \mathbb{Z}\}\) is a subgroup of \(G\).
Proof Use Subgroup Criteria.

Furthermore, \(\langle a \rangle\) is the smallest subgroup of \(G\) that contains \(a\). The subgroup \(\langle a \rangle\) is called the cyclic subgroup generated by \(a\).

title: Slides: Cyclic Groups
text:
Theorem 4.1.9
Theorem. Every cyclic group is abelian.
Proof. Let \(G\) be cyclic. Then \(G=\langle a\rangle\) for some \(a\in G\).
If \(g,h\in G\), then there exist integers \(r\) and \(s\) such that
\(g=a^r\) and \(h=a^s\).
Therefore,
\[
gh=a^ra^s=a^{r+s}=a^{s+r}=a^sa^r=hg.
\]
Hence \(G\) is abelian.

title: Slides: Cyclic Groups
text:
Theorem 4.1.10
Theorem. Every subgroup of a cyclic group is cyclic.

title: Slides: Cyclic Groups
text:
Theorem 4.1.12
Theorem. Let \(G=\langle a\rangle\) be a cyclic group of order \(n\). THen \(a^k=e\) if and only if \(n\) divides \(k\).

title: Slides: Cyclic Groups
text:
Theorem 4.1.13
Theorem. Let \(G=\langle a\rangle\) be a cyclic group of order \(n\). If \(b=a^k\) then the order of \(b\) is \(\frac{n}{d}\) where \(d=gcd(k,n)\).

Thus the possible orders of elements in a finite cyclic group are precisely the positive divisors of the order of the group. If \(k\) is relatively prime to \(n\) then \(G=\langle b\rangle\).

title: Slides: Alternating and Dihedral Groups
text:
Definition of a Group
A group \((G,\cdot)\) is a set \(G\) together with a law of composition
\((a,b)\mapsto a\cdot b\) satisfying:

Associativity:
\((a\cdot b)\cdot c=a\cdot(b\cdot c)\) for \(a,b,c\in G\).
Identity:
There exists \(e\in G\) such that \(e\cdot a=a\cdot e=a\) for every \(a\in G\).
Inverses:
For each \(a\in G\), there exists \(a^{-1}\in G\) such that \(a\cdot a^{-1}=a^{-1}\cdot a=e\).

title: Slides: Alternating and Dihedral Groups
text:
Definition of a Subgroup
Let \(G\) be a group.
A subgroup \(H\) of \(G\) is a subset \(H\) of \(G\) such that when the group operation of \(G\) is restricted to \(H\), \(H\) is a group in its own right.
We write \(H \leq G\).
A subgroup uses the same operation as the original group.

Proposition 3.3.7 Subgroup Criterion
A subset \(H\) of \(G\) is a subgroup if and only if it satisfies the following conditions.

Closure If \(h_1,h_2\in H\), then
\[

Inverse If \(h\in H\), then

\]

title: Slides: Alternating and Dihedral Groups

Let \(H\) be a subset of a group \(G\).

\[
gh^{-1}\in H.

Identity: \(gg^{-1}=e\in H\)
Inverse: \(eg^{-1}=g^{-1}\in H\)

If \(a,b\in H\), then \(a=2m,\qquad b=2n\) for some \(m,n\in\mathbb Z\).
Therefore \(a-b=2m-2n=2(m-n)\in2\mathbb Z\).
Hence \(2\mathbb Z\leq\mathbb Z\).

We write \(f(a)=b\) if \(b\) is the unique element of \(B\) associated with \(a\).

\(A\) is the domain of \(f\).

Surjective Functions
Let \(f:A\to B\) be a function.
The function \(f\) is onto or surjective if every element in \(B\) is the image of some element in \(A\).
That is, for every \(b\in B\), there exists an \(a\in A\) such that \(f(a)=b\).
Sometimes you will this way of expressing onto functions, \(f(A)=B\).

Let \(f:A\to B\) be a function.
The function \(f\) is one-to-one or injective if \(f(a_1)=f(a_2)\) implies \(a_1=a_2\).
That is each element in the image comes from a unique element in the domain.

Let \(R \subset X \times X\) be a relation on \(X\).
The relation \(R\) is an equivalence relation when:

Reflexive: \((x,x) \in R\) for all \(x \in X\).
Symmetric: If \((x,y) \in R\), then \((y,x) \in R\).
Transitive: If \((x,y) \in R\) and \((y,z) \in R\), then \((x,z) \in R\).

text:
Well Ordering of the Natural Numbers
A set \(S\) is well-ordered if every nonempty subset of \(S\) contains a least element.
Principle of Well-Ordering. Every nonempty subset of the natural numbers is well-ordered.
In this class the natural numbers are \(\mathbb{N}=\{0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots\}\).

text:
What about the integers?
The integers \(\mathbb{Z}\) are not well-ordered.
For example,
\[

\]
has no least element.
crumbs: Slides: Equivalence Relations and Division Algorithm

title: Slides: Equivalence Relations and Division Algorithm
text:
Division Algorithm
Division Algorithm. Let \(a\) and \(b\) be integers, with \(b>0\). Then there exist unique integers \(q\) and \(r\) such that \(a=bq+r\) where \(0\leq r<b\).
The proof has three parts:

Existence: Show that \(q\) and \(r\) exist.
\(0\leq r<b\)
Uniqueness: Show that no other \(q\) and \(r\) can satisfy these conditions.
crumbs: Slides: Equivalence Relations and Division Algorithm

title: Slides: Equivalence Relations and Division Algorithm
text:
Division Algorithm: Existence
Let \(S=\{a-bk:k\in\mathbb Z\text{ and }a-bk\geq 0\}.\) If \(0\in S\), then \(b\) divides \(a\), and we can let
\[
q=\frac{a}{b}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
r=0.
\]
Suppose \(0\notin S\). We first show that \(S\) is nonempty. If \(a>0\), then \(a-b\cdot 0\in S\). If \(a<0\), then \(a-b(2a)=a(1-2b)\in S\) Thus \(S\neq\varnothing\).
crumbs: Slides: Equivalence Relations and Division Algorithm

title: Slides: Equivalence Relations and Division Algorithm
text:
Division Algorithm: Existence
By the Principle of Well-Ordering, \(S\) has a smallest member, say
\[
r=a-bq.
\]
Therefore,
\[
a=bq+r
\]
and \(r\geq 0\).
We now show that \(r<b\).
Suppose that \(r>b\). Then
\[
a-b(q+1)=a-bq-b=r-b>0.
\]
Thus \(a-b(q+1)\in S\), but
\[
a-b(q+1)<a-bq=r,
\]
contradicting the fact that \(r\) is the smallest member of \(S\).
Hence \(r\leq b\). Since \(0\notin S\), \(r\neq b\), and therefore
\[
0\leq r<b.
\]
crumbs: Slides: Equivalence Relations and Division Algorithm

title: Slides: Equivalence Relations and Division Algorithm
text:
Division Algorithm: Uniqueness
Suppose there exist integers \(r,r',q,q'\) such that
\[
a=bq+r,\qquad 0\leq r<b
\]
and
\[
a=bq'+r',\qquad 0\leq r'<b.
\]
Then
\[
bq+r=bq'+r'.
\]
Assume that \(r'\geq r\). Then
\[
b(q-q')=r'-r.
\]
Therefore \(b\) divides \(r'-r\), but
\[
0\leq r'-r\leq r'<b.
\]
This is possible only if
\[
r'-r=0.
\]
Hence \(r=r'\) and \(q=q'\).
crumbs: Slides: Equivalence Relations and Division Algorithm

Theorem 1.2.20.
A mapping is invertible if and only if it is both one-to-one and onto.

In other words,
\[
f \text{ is invertible}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
f \text{ is injective and surjective}.

title: Slides: Equivalence Relations and Division Algorithm
text:
Composition of Mappings
Theorem 1.2.15.
Let \(f:A\to B\), \(g:B\to C\), and \(h:C\to D\). Then

The composition of mappings is associative; that is, \((h\circ g)\circ f=h\circ(g\circ f)\).
If \(f\) and \(g\) are both one-to-one, then the mapping \(g\circ f\) is one-to-one.
If \(f\) and \(g\) are both onto, then the mapping \(g\circ f\) is onto.
If \(f\) and \(g\) are bijective, then so is \(g\circ f\).

title: Slides: Properties of Groups and Subgroups
text:
Definition of a Group
A group \((G,\circ)\) is a set \(G\) together with a law of composition
\((a,b)\mapsto a\cdot b\) satisfying:

Associativity:
\((a\cdot b)\cdot c=a\cdot(b\cdot c)\) for \(a,b,c\in G\).
Identity:
There exists \(e\in G\) such that \(e\cdot a=a\cdot e=a\) for every \(a\in G\).
Inverses:
For each \(a\in G\), there exists \(a^{-1}\in G\) such that \(a\cdot a^{-1}=a^{-1}\cdot a=e\).

text:
Proposition 3.2.10 — Uniqueness of Identity
The identity element in a group \(G\) is unique.

Suppose \(e\) and \(e'\) are both identity elements.
Since \(e\) is an identity, \(ee'=e'\).
Since \(e'\) is an identity, \(ee'=e\).
Therefore, \(e=ee'=e'\).
crumbs: Slides: Properties of Groups and Subgroups

title: Slides: Properties of Groups and Subgroups
text:
Proposition 3.2.11 — Uniqueness of the Inverse
If \(g\) is any element in a group \(G\), then its inverse \(g^{-1}\) is unique.

Suppose \(g'\) and \(g''\) are both inverses of \(g\).
Then \(gg'=g'g=e\) and \(gg''=g''g=e\).
Therefore, \(g'=g'e=g'(gg'')=(g'g)g''=eg''=g''\).
crumbs: Slides: Properties of Groups and Subgroups

title: Slides: Properties of Groups and Subgroups
text:
Proposition 3.2.12 — Inverse of a Product
Let \(G\) be a group. If \(a,b\in G\), then \((ab)^{-1}=b^{-1}a^{-1}\).

Indeed,
\(abb^{-1}a^{-1}=aea^{-1}=aa^{-1}=e\),
and similarly,
\(b^{-1}a^{-1}ab=e\).
Thus \(b^{-1}a^{-1}\) is the inverse of \(ab\).
crumbs: Slides: Properties of Groups and Subgroups

title: Slides: Properties of Groups and Subgroups
text:
Proposition 3.2.13 — Inverse of an Inverse
Let \(G\) be a group. For any \(a\in G\), \((a^{-1})^{-1}=a\).

Since
\(a^{-1}(a^{-1})^{-1}=e\),
we obtain
\((a^{-1})^{-1}=e(a^{-1})^{-1}=aa^{-1}(a^{-1})^{-1}=ae=a\).
crumbs: Slides: Properties of Groups and Subgroups

title: Slides: Properties of Groups and Subgroups
text:
Proposition 3.2.14
Let \(G\) be a group and let \(a,b\in G\). Then the equations \(ax=b\) and \(xa=b\) have unique solutions in \(G\).

For \(ax=b\),
\(x=a^{-1}b\).
For \(xa=b\),
\(x=ba^{-1}\).
crumbs: Slides: Properties of Groups and Subgroups

title: Slides: Properties of Groups and Subgroups
text:
Proposition 3.2.15
If \(G\) is a group and \(a,b,c\in G\), then
\(ba=ca\quad\Longrightarrow\quad b=c\)
and
\(ab=ac\quad\Longrightarrow\quad b=c\).

These are the right and left cancellation laws for groups.
For example,
\(ba=ca\quad\Longrightarrow\quad baa^{-1}=caa^{-1}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad b=c\).

Let \(G\) be a group.
A subgroup \(H\) of \(G\) is a subset \(H\) of \(G\) such that when the group operation of \(G\) is restricted to \(H\), \(H\) is a group in its own right.

title: Slides: Definitions and Examples of Groups
text:
Definition of a Group
A group \((G,\circ)\) is a set \(G\) together with a law of composition \((a,b)\mapsto a\circ b\) satisfying:

Associativity:
\((a\circ b)\circ c=a\circ(b\circ c)\) for \(a,b,c\in G\).
Identity:
There exists \(e\in G\) such that \(e\circ a=a\circ e=a\) for every \(a\in G\).
Inverses:
For each \(a\in G\), there exists \(a^{-1}\in G\) such that \(a\circ a^{-1}=a^{-1}\circ a=e\).

title: Slides: Definitions and Examples of Groups
text:
Additional Definitions
A group is abelian (or commutative) if \(a\circ b=b\circ a\) for all \(a,b\in G\).
A Cayley table is a table that shows the result of the group operation for all pairs of elements in the group. We use it to verify that every element has an inverse. If the Caley table is symmetric about the diagonal, then the group is abelian.
The order of a group is the number of elements in the group. Groups can be finite or infinite.

Group of Complex Numbers Under Multiplication
Let \(\mathbb C^\ast\) be the set of nonzero complex numbers.
Under multiplication, \(\mathbb C^\ast\) forms a group.

Identity: \(1\).

The group \(\mathbb C^\ast\) is abelian.

Proposition 3.2.10 — Uniqueness of Identity
The identity element in a group \(G\) is unique.

Suppose \(e\) and \(e'\) are both identity elements.
Since \(e\) is an identity, \(ee'=e'\).
Since \(e'\) is an identity, \(ee'=e\).
Therefore, \(e=ee'=e'\).

title: Slides: Definitions and Examples of Groups
text:
Proposition 3.2.11 — Uniqueness of the Inverse
If \(g\) is any element in a group \(G\), then its inverse \(g^{-1}\) is unique.

Suppose \(g'\) and \(g''\) are both inverses of \(g\).
Then \(gg'=g'g=e\) and \(gg''=g''g=e\).
Therefore, \(g'=g'e=g'(gg'')=(g'g)g''=eg''=g''\).

Division Algorithm
Division Algorithm. Let \(a\) and \(b\) be integers, with \(b>0\). Then there exist unique integers \(q\) and \(r\) such that \(a=bq+r\) where \(0\leq r<b\).
The proof has three parts:

Existence: Show that \(q\) and \(r\) exist.
Verify \(0\leq r<b\)
Uniqueness: Show that no other \(q\) and \(r\) can satisfy these conditions.

text:
Proposition 3.1.4.
Let \(\mathbb Z_n\) be the set of equivalence classes of the integers mod \(n\) and \(a,b,c \in \mathbb Z_n\).

Addition and multiplication are commutative:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a+b &\equiv b+a \pmod n \\
ab &\equiv ba \pmod n.
\end{aligned}
\]

Addition and multiplication are associative:

\[
\begin{aligned}
(a+b)+c &\equiv a+(b+c)\pmod n \\
(ab)c &\equiv a(bc)\pmod n.
\end{aligned}
\]

title: Slides: Integer Equivalence Classes and Symmetries
text:
Proposition 3.1.4. Continued

There are both additive and multiplicative identities:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a+0 &\equiv a \pmod n \\
a\cdot 1 &\equiv a \pmod n.
\end{aligned}
\]

Multiplication distributes over addition:

\[
a(b+c)\equiv ab+ac\pmod n.
\]

text:

\[
a+(-a)\equiv 0\pmod n.
\]

Let \(a\) be a nonzero integer. Then \(\gcd(a,n)=1\) if and only if there exists a multiplicative inverse \(b\) for \(a\pmod n\); that is, a nonzero integer \(b\) such that

\[
ab\equiv 1\pmod n.

title: Equivalence Relations
text:
Define a relation \(\sim\) on \(\mathbb{N}\) via \(a \sim b\) if and only if \(a-b=3k\), for some \(k \in \mathbb{Z}\). Is \(\sim\) an equivalence relation? If so, what are the equivalence classes?

Define a relation \(\sim\) on \(\mathbb{Z}\) via \(a \sim b\) if and only if \(|a|=|b|\). Is \(\sim\) an equivalence relation? If so, what are the equivalence classes?
Define a relation \(\sim\) on \(\mathbb{Z}\) via \(a \sim b\) if and only if \(ab>0\). Is \(\sim\) an equivalence relation? If so, what are the equivalence classes?
Let \(S\) be the set of all subsets of \(\mathbb{Z}\). Define a relation \(\sim\) on \(S\) via \(T \sim U\) if and only if \(T \subseteq U\). Is \(\sim\) an equivalence relation? If so, what are the equivalence classes?
Let \(S\) be the set of all subsets of \(\mathbb{R}\). Define a relation \(\sim\) on \(S\) via \(x \sim y\) in \(\mathbb{R}\) if \(x \ge y\). Is \(\sim\) an equivalence relation? If so, what are the equivalence classes?

Let \(S\) be the set of all subsets of \(\mathbb{Z}\). Define a relation \(\sim\) on \(S\) via \(m \sim n\) in \(\mathbb{Z}\) if \(m \equiv n \pmod{6}\). Is \(\sim\) an equivalence relation? If so, what are the equivalence classes?

title: Math 393 Syllabus
text:
Groups, rings, and fields! Oh My! These are the core algebraic structures in mathematics. Finally we get to the good stuff: axiomatic mathematics and discussing the rules and structures that are the baseline tools for all of mathematics. Groups describe symmetry and have rich and interesting structure that arise from 3 simple axioms.



Prerequisite: MATH 240 and MATH 310
Groups, rings, and fields, the basic algebraic structures in contemporary mathematics.



The best way to get in touch with me is in-person or by email. In general, if you have any difficulties with the material, schedule, or anything else, get in touch with me. I’m here to help, and it’s much easier to help if you are proactive. If my office hours don’t work for you, email me and we can work out a time to me in-person or via Zoom.




Discuss the basic algebraic structures appearing in mathematics today
Apply the knowledge of these structures to the analysis of concrete special cases
Compute degrees of extensions
Prove impossibility of certain ruler and compass geometric constructions, e.g. squaring of the circle
Parametrize field extensions by groups and vice-versa
Determine the solvability of higher degree polynomial equations by radicals
Express concepts and techniques of Abstract Algebra in oral and written form

On each homework assignment, please indicate which students you worked with. An important part of mathematical culture and work is acknowledging the people that helped you understand and solve a problem.
